title: Flamethrowers, Boycotts, and a Floating Piano: Inside Eurovision’s Chaotic 70th Final
summary:
Picture a stage where a classical violinist shreds beside a pop star while actual flames shoot from her instrument. That was Finland’s entry at Saturday’s Eurovision grand final in Vienna—and it almost won the whole thing. But the 70th edition of the world’s campiest song contest was about more than just pyro and power ballads.

Twenty-five acts competed at the Wiener Stadthalle arena, from a Serbian metal band to a Moldovan folk rapper named Satoshi, whose high-energy “Viva, Moldova” carried a subtle pro-European Union message. Greece’s Akylas offered a playful critique of consumerism with “Ferto” (“Bring It”), nodding to the country’s lingering financial scars. And Australia’s Delta Goodrem, a genuine star Down Under, delivered a showstopping “Eclipse” while suspended above a glittering piano—a performance so slick it pushed her up the betting odds.

But Eurovision, often called the World Cup of pop, couldn’t escape geopolitics. For the third consecutive year, Israel’s participation sparked fury over its military actions in Gaza. Five longtime competitors—Spain, the Netherlands, Ireland, Iceland, and Slovenia—boycotted entirely, shrinking the field to its smallest since 2003. Outside, pro-Palestinian demonstrators staged a concert under the banner “No stage for genocide.” Inside, four protesters were ejected after trying to disrupt Israeli singer Noam Bettan’s semifinal performance.

“Inviting Israel on such a beautiful stage is an affront to all who believe in humanity,” said organizer Patrick Bongola. Yet historian Dean Vuletic notes that political firestorms are nothing new: Austria itself boycotted in 1969 over Spain’s dictatorship.

Finland’s “Liekinheitin” (“Flamethrower”)—a duet between pop singer Pete Parkkonen and violinist Linda Lampenius—was the bookies’ favorite. But Eurovision has a soft spot for underdogs. “People like to see the artist-in-the-making or an artist from a smaller, poorer country,” Vuletic said. In the end, the voting system—a baffling mix of public televotes and professional juries—crowned a surprise winner. (Spoiler: it wasn’t Finland.)

With 166 million viewers last year and a planned Asian spinoff, Eurovision keeps growing—flames, protests, and all.
why_it_matters: Eurovision’s controversies show how cultural events can become platforms for political protest, helping you understand how art and global issues intertwine and why representation matters in public spectacles.

background_read: The Eurovision Song Contest began in 1956 as a post-war effort to bring European nations together through live music broadcasts.
Since then, it has often reflected real-world politics: Greece and Turkey have used it to express national pride, and Russia’s participation has fuelled debates.

Wiener Stadthalle (a major indoor arena in Vienna, Austria’s capital) hosted this year’s final, and Dean Vuletic, a historian who studies how politics and Eurovision intersect, has noted that political firestorms are nothing new—Austria itself boycotted the 1969 contest to protest Spain’s dictatorship under Francisco Franco.

The contest’s famous voting system—a mix of public telephone votes and professional music-industry juries—can produce surprising winners, sometimes from smaller nations like Ukraine (which won in 2004 and 2016).
Israel began competing in 1973 and has increasingly faced protests over its government’s actions, with several countries boycotting in recent years.

perspectives.description: Fans loved the bold fusion of classical violin and pop, seeing it as proof that Eurovision encourages creative risk-taking and can help smaller countries gain global attention.

Protesters and boycotters argued that including Israel while its military operates in Gaza normalises violence and betrays Eurovision’s supposedly apolitical mission, making the contest complicit in suffering.

Scholars like Dean Vuletic note that political rows are nothing new; Eurovision has weathered similar storms since the 1960s, and each controversy forces the organising union to clarify its rules about political messages.

With a planned Asian spinoff and record viewership, Eurovision’s growing commercial power means it will likely face more pressure to balance inclusivity with human-rights concerns, possibly reshaping how the contest screens participants.
